standard.text: Recognize a statistical question as one that anticipates variability in the answers.

vocabulary.def: A question you expect different answers to, such as "How tall are the students in this class?"
A number line with one dot stacked above a value for each time it appears in the data.
What one equal step on a number line is worth.

variants.prompt: Order 15, 8, 22, 11, 4. On a line from 0 to 40 split into 4 equal jumps, what is one jump worth?
Order 6, 1, 9, 3, 7. On a line from 0 to 100 split into 10 equal jumps, what is one jump worth?

errors.means: The student is counting tick marks instead of dividing the total span by the number of intervals.
errors.do: Draw the same line labeled 0 to 100 with 5 jumps. Ask whether one jump can still be worth 1.

errors.shows: Ordered list keeps the original order
errors.means: The student read "order" as "copy" and did not compare values pairwise.
errors.do: Hand out five index cards with the numbers and have the student physically arrange them left to right.

steps: Draw a blank line. Label only the two endpoints, 0 and 10.
Mark the 5 equal jumps. Ask: "How many jumps? How much distance total?"
Write 10 ÷ 5 = 2 under the line and label every tick: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10.
Change the endpoint to 20 and repeat. Students say the new jump value before you write it.

2-1.frame: One jump is worth ___ because the distance from ___ to ___ is split into ___ equal parts.

extension.prompt: A line runs from 0 to 30 with 6 equal jumps. Where does 25 sit — on a tick mark or between two?
extension.answer: One jump = 30 ÷ 6 = 5, so ticks are 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30. The value 25 lands exactly on a tick mark.

standard.text: Display numerical data in plots on a number line, including dot plots, histograms, and box plots.

vocabulary.def: A graph of how many data values fall inside each equal-width interval.
A range of values, such as 10–19, that collects data into one bar.
How many values land in one interval.

variants.prompt: Which interval holds 40: 30–39 or 40–49? How many of 12, 35, 41, 44, 58 land in 40–49?
variants.answer: 40 belongs in 40–49. Values in 40–49: 41 and 44 — a frequency of 2.

variants.prompt: Which interval holds 60: 50–59 or 60–69? How many of 51, 60, 64, 70, 72 land in 60–69?
variants.answer: 60 belongs in 60–69. Values in 60–69: 60 and 64 — a frequency of 2.

errors.means: The student is reading the upper endpoint as the start of the next bin.
errors.do: Write the bins as a number line strip and shade 20–29 in one color. Point to where 29 physically sits.

errors.shows: A value counted in two bins
errors.means: The student has not internalized that bins must not overlap.
errors.do: Tally the full data set aloud together, crossing off each value as it is placed exactly once.

steps: Write the bins 0–9, 10–19, 20–29, 30–39 across the board.
Read five values one at a time; students point to the correct bin before you write a tally.
Total the tallies and check the sum equals the number of values read.
Ask: "Could any value have gone in two bins? Why not?"

2-2.frame: The value ___ belongs in the interval ___ because it is at least ___ and at most ___.

extension.prompt: A data set has 24 values sorted into bins with frequencies 5, 8, 6, and ___. What is the missing frequency?

standard.text: Report the median and describe what it says about the data set.

vocabulary.def: The middle value once the data are in order.
The number halfway between two values; add them and divide by 2.
A data set with no single middle value, so the two middle values are averaged.

variants.prompt: Put in order: 14, 6, 21, 9, 17. What number is halfway between 20 and 25?
Put in order: 30, 12, 25, 18, 21. What number is halfway between 8 and 15?

errors.shows: Halfway between 12 and 17 given as 14 or 15
errors.means: The student rounded away the decimal rather than dividing an odd sum by 2.
errors.do: Put 12 and 17 on a number line and count in one step from each end at a time until the steps meet.

errors.shows: Median read off the unordered list
errors.means: The student took the physically middle number, not the middle value.
errors.do: Require the ordered list to be written before the median is circled, every time.

steps: Write five numbers out of order. Students rewrite them in order on whiteboards.
Cross off one value from each end in turn until one remains. Name it the median.
Repeat with six numbers so two remain. Ask: "Now what?"
Write (a + b) ÷ 2 and compute the midpoint together.

2-3.frame: The median is ___ because after ordering, ___ values sit below it and ___ sit above it.

extension.prompt: A set of six values has median 10. The four values 4, 8, 12, 16 are known. Give one possible pair for the other two.
extension.answer: Many answers. The two middle values must average 10 — for example, adding 2 and 20 gives ordered 2, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 with median (8 + 12) ÷ 2 = 10.

standard.text: Display numerical data in plots on a number line, including box plots.

vocabulary.def: A five-number picture of a data set: minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum.
The median of the lower half (Q1) or the upper half (Q3) of an ordered set.
The minimum, Q1, median, Q3, and maximum together.

variants.prompt: Ordered: 2, 6, 9, 11, 15, 19, 22, 28. Find the median of the lower half.
Ordered: 4, 7, 10, 13, 18, 20. Find the median of the upper half.

errors.means: The student named a position instead of computing the median of the lower half.
errors.do: Box the lower half on the board and run the same cross-off-from-both-ends routine used for the median.

errors.shows: The overall median included in both halves
errors.means: The student is splitting an even set as if it were odd.
errors.do: Count the values first. Say aloud: "Eight values, so four and four, and nothing is left in the middle."

steps: Write eight ordered values. Draw a vertical line between the fourth and fifth.
Find the median of the whole set from the two middle values.
Treat the lower four as their own small set and find its median. Label it Q1.
Repeat on the upper four for Q3, then read the five-number summary aloud.

2-4.frame: Q1 is ___ because it is the median of the lower half, which contains ___ .

extension.prompt: A box plot has min 3, Q1 7, median 12, Q3 18, max 25. Between which two values do the middle half of the data sit?
extension.answer: Between Q1 = 7 and Q3 = 18. That middle 50% spans 18 − 7 = 11 units.

standard.text: Report measures of variability, including range and interquartile range.

vocabulary.def: Maximum minus minimum — the full spread.
Q3 minus Q1 — the spread of the middle half.
How spread out the values are.

variants.prompt: Range of 23, 8, 41, 16, 30? If Q1 = 12 and Q3 = 35, what is Q3 − Q1?
Range of 100, 62, 85, 71, 94? If Q1 = 68 and Q3 = 92, what is Q3 − Q1?

errors.means: The student subtracted the first two numbers listed rather than finding the maximum and minimum.
errors.do: Require circling the largest and smallest values before any subtraction is written.

errors.means: The student subtracted in the order the numbers were given.
errors.do: Write "bigger minus smaller" above the board work; a spread is never negative.

steps: Post five values. Students circle the max and box the min.
Write range = max − min and compute together.
Give Q1 and Q3 directly. Ask which is bigger before subtracting.
Ask: "Which spread ignores the extremes — range or IQR?"

2-5.frame: The range is ___ because the largest value is ___ and the smallest is ___ .

extension.prompt: Two classes both have range 20, but Class A has IQR 4 and Class B has IQR 16. What does that tell you?
extension.answer: The middle half of Class A's data spans 4 units; the middle half of Class B's spans 16 units, so B has the larger spread within its middle half. Both full data sets span 20 units. These summaries alone do not tell us how many outliers there are or how values are distributed within those spans.

standard.text: Fluently divide multi-digit numbers using the standard algorithm.

vocabulary.def: The amount being divided.
The number you divide by.
The result of a division.
The amount left after making equal whole-number groups; it must be less than the divisor.

variants.answer: 252 ÷ 7 = 36. Divide 25 tens by 7 to get 3 tens with 4 tens remaining; 42 ones ÷ 7 = 6 ones. Check: 36 × 7 = 252.
325 ÷ 5 = 65. Divide 32 tens by 5 to get 6 tens with 2 tens remaining; 25 ones ÷ 5 = 5 ones. Check: 65 × 5 = 325.

errors.means: The student stopped before regrouping and dividing the remaining amount. The remainder is larger than the divisor.
errors.do: Exchange the remaining 3 tens for 30 ones. Combine with the 6 ones. Divide all 36 ones into six groups.

errors.means: The student treated the 2 tens as a hundreds digit when writing the quotient.
errors.do: Label the quotient places tens and ones. Two tens and six ones make 26, then check 26 × 6.

steps: Estimate 156 ÷ 6 using 120 ÷ 6 = 20 and 180 ÷ 6 = 30; the quotient should be between 20 and 30.
Represent 156 as 15 tens and 6 ones. Share the tens among six groups: each gets 2 tens and 3 tens remain.
Rename the 3 tens as 30 ones. Combine with 6 ones and divide 36 ones into six groups. Each gets 6 ones.
Record the algorithm with quotient 26. Check 6 × 26 = 156. Ask a partner to explain the place value of the 2.

2-6.frame: I divided ___ by ___ and got ___. I checked by multiplying ___ by ___ and adding any remainder.

extension.prompt: There are 347 students. Each bus seats at most 24 students. What is the fewest buses needed? Explain how the remainder affects your answer.
extension.answer: 347 ÷ 24 = 14 remainder 11, because 24 × 14 = 336. The 11 remaining students need another bus, so 15 buses are needed.

standard.text: Fluently add, subtract, multiply, and divide multi-digit decimals using the standard algorithm.

vocabulary.def: The number being divided.
The number you are dividing by.
Write a zero at the end of a decimal so the division can continue.

errors.means: The student shifted one place instead of two.
errors.do: Write the digits in a place-value chart and slide them two columns left, filling the empty column with a zero.

errors.means: The student divided the digits separately and lost the decimal alignment.
errors.do: Set the problem up vertically with the decimal point carried straight up into the quotient before dividing.

steps: Draw a place-value chart from thousands to thousandths.
Place 0.6 in it. Multiply by 10, then by 10 again, sliding the digit each time.
State the rule: multiplying moves digits left, dividing moves them right.
Do 4.5 ÷ 10 and 0.07 × 1000 the same way.

2-7.frame: Multiplying by 100 moves each digit ___ places to the ___, so ___ becomes ___ .

extension.prompt: Why does 4.8 ÷ 0.2 give the same answer as 48 ÷ 2?
extension.answer: Multiplying both the dividend and the divisor by 10 does not change the quotient; it only rewrites the problem with a whole-number divisor. Both equal 24.

standard.text: Report the mean and describe what it says about the data set.

vocabulary.def: The sum of the values divided by how many values there are.
Another way to read the mean: the amount each value would get if the total were shared evenly.
The amount still needed to reach a target total.

variants.prompt: Mean of 20, 18, 25, 17? What must be added to 72 to reach 100?
Mean of 9, 15, 6, 12, 18? What must be added to 55 to reach 90?

errors.shows: The sum reported as the mean
errors.means: The student stopped after the addition step.
errors.do: Require both numbers to be written and labeled: "total = ___, how many = ___" before dividing.

errors.means: The student miscounted the values, often by skipping a repeat.
errors.do: Number the values 1, 2, 3 … above them before summing.

steps: Stack five towers of cubes of different heights.
Move cubes until every tower is the same height. That height is the mean.
Now do it numerically: add, count, divide. Compare to the cube answer.
Ask: "If one tower grew by 5, what happens to the mean?"

2-8.frame: The mean is ___ because the total ___ is shared evenly among ___ values.

extension.prompt: Four scores have a mean of 85. Three of them are 80, 90, and 88. What is the fourth?
extension.answer: Total must be 4 × 85 = 340. The known three sum to 258, so the fourth is 340 − 258 = 82.

standard.text: Report the mean absolute deviation and describe variability.

vocabulary.def: The average distance of the values from the mean.
How far one value sits from the mean.
A distance reported as a positive number, no matter the direction.

variants.prompt: The mean is 30. How far is 37 from the mean? How far is 22?
The mean is 50. How far is 50 from the mean? How far is 43?

errors.shows: Distance of 14 from a mean of 20 given as −6
errors.means: The student subtracted without treating distance as non-negative.
errors.do: Point at both values on a number line and count the jumps aloud; a count of jumps is never negative.

errors.means: The student produced the total deviation rather than the mean deviation.
errors.do: Name the M in MAD: it is a mean, so the last step is always a division by the count.

steps: Mark the mean on a number line with a triangle.
Plot each data value and draw an arrow back to the mean. Label each arrow's length.
Sum the arrow lengths, then divide by how many arrows there are.
Ask: "What would MAD be if every value equalled the mean?"

2-9.frame: The distance from ___ to the mean is ___ because distance counts jumps, not direction.

extension.prompt: A set has mean 10 and MAD 0. What must be true of the data?
extension.answer: Every value equals 10. A MAD of zero means no value deviates from the mean at all.

standard.text: Relate the choice of measures of center and variability to the shape of the distribution.

vocabulary.def: A distribution stretched further on one side than the other.
A distribution that looks about the same on both sides of the center.
The number that best represents the middle of the data.

variants.prompt: Which measure of center fits 5, 6, 6, 7, 80 — mean or median? Why?
variants.answer: Median (6). The mean is 104 ÷ 5 = 20.8, which is larger than four of the five values because 80 pulls it up.

variants.prompt: Which measure of center fits 41, 44, 45, 46, 49 — mean or median? Why?
variants.answer: Either works. The data are symmetric with no outlier; the mean (45) and median (45) agree.

errors.shows: Mean chosen for an obviously skewed set
errors.means: The student is applying a default rather than reading the shape.
errors.do: Compute both, then ask which number more students in the data set are actually near.

errors.shows: Median chosen for a symmetric set with a stated reason of "outliers"
errors.means: The student is applying the outlier rule without checking whether an outlier exists.
errors.do: Ask the student to point at the outlier. If they cannot, the rule does not apply.

steps: Post two data sets: one symmetric, one with a single extreme value.
Compute mean and median for both and record in a 2 × 2 table.
Circle the pair that disagrees and ask why.
State the decision rule in students' own words and post it.

2-10.frame: I would report the ___ because the data are ___, and the ___ is pulled by ___ .

extension.prompt: Give a data set of five values where mean and median are equal but the range is 40.
extension.answer: Many answers. For example 10, 25, 30, 35, 50: mean = 150 ÷ 5 = 30, median = 30, range = 50 − 10 = 40.
